extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate CS/mathematics students learning proof techniques (CS103 Winter 2018)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and style rules for composing correct, clear mathematical-induction proofs about natural numbers and discrete structures; covers choosing P(n), base cases, inductive step, directionality, and when to use complete induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define some predicate P(n)
rubrics_metrics.description: When writing an inductive proof, spell out explicitly what predicate P(n) you'll prove by induction (e.g., 'P(n) is the statement “any 2^n × 2^n grid missing a square can be tiled with right triominoes.”').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin your proof by spelling out what predicate you'll be proving something about by induction. Treat P(n) as a predicate (a logical assertion about n), not as a number or algebraic expression. If you're having trouble, the handout's 'A Guide to P(n)' gives examples showing how a universal theorem can be encoded as 'for any n, P(n)'.

rubrics_metrics.name: State you'll prove the predicate by induction and specify the domain
rubrics_metrics.description: After defining P(n), explicitly say that you'll prove it by induction and make clear which numbers/cases you intend to cover (e.g., all natural numbers, only even numbers greater than five, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives the reader a heads-up about how the induction will proceed and prevents ambiguity about the scope of the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove base case(s) explicitly and write out what P(0) states
rubrics_metrics.description: All inductive proofs require base case(s). Explicitly write out what P(0) (or the chosen base index) actually states, then prove it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommended phrasing: 'We will prove P(0), which states that ...' or 'For our base case, we'll prove P(0), namely, that …'. Choosing an appropriate base case ensures you haven't omitted initial values and clarifies what must be shown at the foundation of the induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose the simplest possible base case and check boundary cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer the absolute simplest base case (often n=0) because it ensures the theorem covers all desired n and can reveal boundary cases where the theorem fails.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons: (1) ensures truth for every natural number including zero; (2) base case should be as simplified as possible because the inductive step uses simplification; (3) choosing simplest exposes boundary exceptions (e.g., subdivision into 0 squares may be false); (4) can shorten proof if base case is minimal. If similar reasoning appears in both base and inductive step, try simplifying the base case further.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set up and prove the inductive step: assume P(k) then prove P(k+1)
rubrics_metrics.description: State the inductive step as the implication 'If P(k) is true, then P(k+1) is true.' Explicitly write out what the assumption P(k) means and what you're going to prove about P(k+1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typically you assume P(k) for an arbitrary k and then derive P(k+1). Writing both sides explicitly clarifies the logic for the reader and helps you confirm what you're assuming versus proving.

rubrics_metrics.name: When the consequent is universal, start with an arbitrary object of size k+1
rubrics_metrics.description: If P(k+1) is a universal statement ('for any object of size k+1 ...'), then in the inductive step you should pick an arbitrary object of size k+1 and show it satisfies the property — not build it by adding elements to a k-sized object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the logical structure of the implication: assume the antecedent (P(k) true), then to prove the universal consequent choose an arbitrary instance of size k+1 and reduce/transform it to an instance covered by the inductive hypothesis (e.g., remove elements to get size k). This avoids the common mistake of 'starting with k and adding elements' which can violate the correct logical flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid proving backwards / do not assume what you are trying to prove
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not begin the inductive step by asserting the very statement you intend to prove (i.e., don't assume P(k+1) to derive P(k)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern shown: assuming 'sum of first k+1 powers of two is 2^{k+1}-1' and manipulating it to arrive at the inductive hypothesis; this reverses implication and is logically invalid. Ensure you assume only P(k) (or the allowed hypotheses) and derive P(k+1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclude the proof explicitly
rubrics_metrics.description: After completing the base case(s) and inductive step, state the conclusion (e.g., 'completing the proof by induction') and close the proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A short concluding remark and end-of-proof symbol (■) are sufficient; explicitly remind the reader that the induction yields the result for all intended n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide between standard induction and complete induction using a heuristic
rubrics_metrics.description: Use standard (weak) induction when you can reduce k+1 to k specifically; use complete (strong) induction when you need assumptions about some smaller number between 0 and k but cannot determine which in advance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heuristic: if you can determine in advance the size of the smaller subproblem, use standard induction; if you can't determine the size in advance (e.g., splitting into two parts of unknown sizes), use complete induction. Complete induction 'supersedes' standard induction but don't use it unless those extra assumptions are actually needed — mirror the structure of your argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mirror the structure of the argument; include only relevant assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose the form of induction that matches the proof's structure and avoid cluttering the proof with unnecessary assumptions (e.g., don't use complete induction if only P(k) is needed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stylistic advice: include only the assumptions that are relevant to the reasoning; this keeps proofs clearer and focused.

rubrics_metrics.name: If you need to reason about several smaller sizes, ensure the inductive hypothesis covers them
rubrics_metrics.description: When the inductive step requires knowledge about sizes smaller than k (not just k), formulate the hypothesis to include all needed smaller cases (i.e., use complete induction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: splitting a tree into two subtrees of unknown sizes between 1 and k requires the hypothesis that P(j) holds for all j ≤ k so you can apply it to each subtree.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write out P(k) and P(k+1) explicitly during the inductive step
rubrics_metrics.description: Make clear to readers (and yourself) exactly what you're assuming and what you're proving by writing the content of P(k) and P(k+1) in words or formulas during the proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This practice reduces ambiguity and helps avoid logical errors such as confusing the assumption with the thing to be proved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the recommended inductive-proof template (structure your proof into steps)
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow a clear structure: (1) define predicate P(n), (2) state you'll prove it by induction and the domain, (3) prove base case(s) explicitly, (4) prove the inductive step (assume P(k), prove P(k+1)), (5) conclude the proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When starting out, adhere closely to this template to produce clear, well-organized inductive proofs; as you gain experience you may relax rigid formatting but retain the logical components.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use base-case choice to simplify and shorten proofs when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: If reasoning in the base case duplicates reasoning in the inductive step, you can often choose a simpler base case to eliminate redundancy and shorten the proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: choosing base case n=0 rather than n=1 when n=0 is valid and makes base case trivial; avoid unnecessarily complex base cases that repeat inductive-step machinery.
